abstract: Hybrid superconducting-semiconducting circuits provide a versatile platform for investigating coherent transport in mesoscopic weak links. Superconducting quantum point contacts (SQPCs) are particularly interesting in this context, as their supercurrent is carried by a discrete number of ballistic transport modes. Here, we investigate a gate-tunable superconducting quantum point contact realized in Ge/SiGe. By incorporating the QPC into a highly asymmetric superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID), we gain access to its current-phase relation (CPR) and switching current, enabling phase-sensitive studies of few-mode superconducting transport. We observe a direct correspondence between conductance quantization and switching-current quantization, linking the normal-state transport modes to the superconducting response. In addition, we demonstrate strong gate tunability of the effective transmission near the onset of the first conductance plateau. Under microwave irradiation, the QPC exhibits photon-assisted multiple Andreev reflections at lower transparencies and Shapiro replicas in the high-transparency, few-mode regime.
title: A superconducting quantum point contact in Ge

abstract: We propose a protocol to measure the non-Hermitian topological invariant associated with the Lindbladian spectrum of chiral-symmetric open Gaussian systems from the relaxation of the covariance matrix. Importantly, the method works in the long-time regime and does not rely on isolating edge modes, so it remains applicable even when the Liouvillian skin effect may obscure them. We illustrate the technique on a Kitaev chain with reservoir-induced nonreciprocity, for which we first obtain a fully analytical and previously unknown description of its topological phase diagram. We then show that our protocol reliably distinguishes all the different phases.
comment: Main text: 6 pages, 1 figure; Supplemental Material: 8 pages
title: Detecting non-Hermitian topology from long-time dynamics

abstract: Finite measurements at a chain end can certify local quantum dynamics without determining bulk topology. We combine Hamiltonian learning with commutator bounds to certify the persistence of localized Majorana operators in Kitaev chains. Time-resolved single-shot boundary measurements and local bond calibrations define joint confidence sets for local Hamiltonian coefficients. Under explicit device assumptions, these sets yield state-independent lower bounds on symmetrized autocorrelations with a prescribed failure probability, valid for all compatible continuations. With equal hopping and pairing on the first bond and no additional boundary terms, an exact identity enables inference from the end qubit alone, even with arbitrary time-independent interactions elsewhere. Synthetic benchmarks near a boundary sweet spot certify persistence for up to about 60 times the measurement window. Three- and six-qubit IBM records strengthen conditional guarantees for the programmed coherent Hamiltonian. Applications to quantum-dot models relate tuning precision to persistence times and detuning-induced splitting.
comment: 37 pages, including 17 pages of main text and 20 pages of supplemental material; 10 figures
title: Certifying Majorana persistence through Hamiltonian learning from boundary measurements

abstract: Organic semiconductors are attractive for spintronic applications owing to their weak spin-orbit coupling, small hyperfine interactions, mechanical flexibility, and tunable electronic properties. Organic spin valves (OSVs) provide a representative platform for investigating spin-dependent transport. However, the magnetoresistance (MR) response is highly sensitive to the ferromagnetic electrode/organic semiconductor interface (spinterface). Variations in interfacial morphology, chemical interaction, energy-level alignment, and spin polarization can strongly affect spin injection, transport, and detection, making reproducible OSV performance difficult to achieve. Here, we investigate how in situ thermal annealing affects the electrical and magnetotransport properties of complete NDI-based OSVs. Two top-electrode configurations are compared: directly evaporated Co/Au and transferred Gr (graphene)/Co/Au. Both as-cast devices exhibit clear MR responses, with a stronger absolute response observed for the transferred-electrode device. After in situ annealing, the resistance of both device types increases substantially, and no reproducible MR response is resolved, despite the enhanced structural order observed in companion films and an approximately 36-fold increase in the effective vertical conductivity extracted from electron-only devices. This contrasting behavior indicates that improved bulk order alone is insufficient to ensure enhanced spin-valve performance. Instead, annealing-induced changes in interfacial contact, contact homogeneity, and local current distribution can become dominant in determining the complete-device response. These results emphasize the critical role of spinterface stability and interface engineering in achieving reliable and thermally robust OSV operation.
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Supporting Information available as an ancillary PDF
title: Interfacial Effects of Thermal Reorganization on Charge and Spin Transport in Organic Spin Valves

abstract: Measurement-induced transitions of free fermions depend strongly on symmetry, but their interplay with quasiperiodic localization and superconducting pairing remains largely unexplored. We study a continuously monitored model of free fermions with pairing, where quasiperiodicity both controls localization and changes the symmetry class of the monitored field theory. Using topological entanglement entropy as a probe of nonlocal correlations in quantum state diffusion simulations, we identify a transition between a critical phase whose von Neumann entanglement entropy scales as $(\ln L)^2$ and an area-law phase, whereas no transition occurs in the clean limit, consistent with the corresponding DIII and D nonlinear sigma models. The transition line exhibits strong multifractality and depends nonmonotonically on quasiperiodicity, which we associate with the symmetry crossover. Deep in the Zeno regime, we derive an effective non-Hermitian Bogoliubov-de Gennes description of individual trajectories and obtain a closed-form localization length that quantitatively agrees with numerics. Our results reveal how symmetry, quasiperiodic localization, and measurement backaction combine to determine both critical entanglement and microscopic trajectory localization in monitored superconductors.
title: Symmetry-Controlled Criticality and Zeno Localization in a Monitored Quasiperiodic Superconductor

abstract: Two-dimensional electron gases in terahertz cavities are among the most mature platforms for ultrastrong light--matter coupling, yet their collective response is captured by the linear Hopfield model, which has an exact classical correspondence. We show that the intrinsic band nonparabolicity of the electrons, recently revealed through nonlinear diamagnetism, turns this system into a quantum Kerr oscillator that squeezes terahertz light. Using a non-rotating-wave theory with ultrastrong-coupling-consistent input--output, an ab initio cavity bath, and a self-consistent model of electron heating, we predict output squeezing of 1.8--2.4\,dB with present GaAs samples in weakly confined cavities with quality factors of order $10^2$, and up to $\approx9$\,dB with modest improvements in mobility or cavity frequency. Carrier heating sets limits through a material figure of merit, which yields a simple design rule that the optimal cavity quality factor scales inversely with the ultrastrong-coupling strength.
title: Squeezed terahertz light from nonlinear diamagnetism in ultrastrongly coupled two-dimensional electrons

abstract: We study the transport sector of the spinterface model of chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) under spin-resolved dissipation, extending the quantum non-equilibrium Green's function formulation of Ref.~\cite{Alwan2026QSpinterface} to spin-resolved lead broadenings. The spin current decomposes into an achiral part, driven by the interfacial moment, and a chiral part, driven by the Rashba spin flip. Under increasing lead spin asymmetry, the achiral part grows linearly while the chiral part follows the geometric-mean suppression, so the two sectors dissociate; they also peak at different coupling scales along the lead broadening. The coupling and bias optima are operating points of the reference configuration, not universal scaling laws. A structural zero appears at $λ_R\sin(φ/2)=t_{\mathrm{mol}}$ in the collinear-lead configuration, where the chiral signal collapses to machine precision universally across chain lengths, frequency resolutions, and twist angles; the zero originates from the rank-one singular bond matrix, whose null eigenvector traps an electron in a spin-superposition dark state that does not hop. With non-collinear ferromagnetic leads, the zero is broken in a controlled way: the residual is generically linear in the transverse polarization, arising from a single coherent spin flip at a boundary, and becomes quadratic at a tuned cancellation angle where two boundary contributions interfere destructively, with the scaling exponent jumping sharply from one to two. These results establish the spinterface model as a transport platform with a two-axis dissociation structure, non-scaling operating optima, and an exact structural zero whose non-collinear deformation is a clean linear-plus-quadratic hierarchy.
title: Achiral-Chiral Dissociation and Structural Zero of the Current in the Spinterface Model of CISS

abstract: Majorana modes, zero-energy excitations of superconducting wires that are their own antiparticles, could store quantum information protected from local noise. In transport experiments, however, ordinary bound states mimic their signature, a conductance peak at zero voltage, and whether Majorana modes have been observed remains debated. A sign, $Q$, of the electron reflection at zero energy marks the topological phase of a long wire, but what $Q$ certifies in a finite device has been unclear. Here we show for the first time that $Q$ counts reflectionless states, waves that enter through one contact and leave entirely through the other: $Q=-1$ when an odd number of them lie in the lower half of the complex energy plane. In a finite wire this means that the two Majorana modes are split by less than their coupling to the contacts. With equal contacts, every sign change of $Q$, including the bulk topological transition, is an exceptional point at which two such states merge and transmission is maximally flat. At zero temperature, $Q=-1$ exactly when the zero-bias conductance measured at a contact exceeds $e^2/h$. These results show what transport can certify about a Majorana device and how to read the invariant from conductance.
title: Reflection Zeros Set the Scattering Invariant of Finite Majorana Wires

abstract: We study a system of three closely spaced conducting sheets, whose thermal emission largely violates Kirchhoff's law through nonreciprocal frequency conversion enabled by Floquet phenomena. We leverage surface mode transitions controlled by temporal modulation of one of the metasurfaces, resulting in largely asymmetric frequency conversion. Our findings broaden the capabilities of Floquet metasurfaces for wave conversion and energy manipulation, paving the way towards magnet-free nonreciprocal photonic devices with opportunities for thermal management and efficient photonic refrigeration.
title: Asymmetric Frequency Conversion and Violation of Kirchhoff's Law of Thermal Radiation in Phased Floquet Metasurfaces

abstract: Developments in single-molecule imaging and sensing techniques have enabled direct observation of biomolecular dynamics at interfaces, which has important implications for the fields of membrane biophysics, nanofluidic sensing and transport. However, integrating active surface transport, localization and control over molecule motion remains challenging, limiting further progress in the realization of single-molecule devices. Here, we introduce an integrated surface acoustic wave (SAW)-hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) platform as a contactless actuation platform for directional transport of biomolecules over hBN surfaces. hBN provides an atomically flat surface on which DNA can be confined and still retain in-plane mobility, whereas SAW actuation enables active and guided transport without requiring specific electrical, dielectric or magnetic properties of the biomolecules. Trajectory- and jump-based analyses show that increasing the SAW power leads to higher displacement bias in the streaming direction, resulting in transport velocities along increasingly more linearized trajectories. We thus demonstrate that SAWs can induce tunable directional transport of DNA molecules confined on hBN surfaces, providing a new approach for the on-chip manipulation of biomolecules in nanofluidic systems. Our findings have important implications for the development of advanced single-molecule sequencing platforms and other technologies for biomolecular manipulation and analysis.
title: Acoustically driven motion of single molecules at hBN surfaces

abstract: Quantum scattering is a fundamental probe of the scattering region and the quantum dynamics of outgoing particles. In two terminals, the statistics of non-interacting fermions is described by a generalized binomial distribution, that arises from the Pauli exclusion principle, while deviations are a signature of interactions. In this work, we extend this result to a scattering region coupled to three outgoing terminals (or channels), obtaining exact bounds for the statistics of the outgoing fermions. In particular, for two fermions and three terminals, four inequalities involving six measured probabilities determine whether a non-interacting scatterer can explain the observed statistics. Applying these inequalities to recent scattering experiments in cold atoms, we are able to identify a regime where interactions have a significant contribution on the outgoing particles. Therefore, our work opens up the possibility of identifying fermion interactions at the nanoscale in systems that range from mesoscopic conductors to optical traps in cold atoms.
comment: 5 pages of main text, 2 figures. Supplementary information and code are available in the GitHub repository cited as Ref. [84] in the manuscript
title: Exact characterization of three-terminal fermion counting under one-body scattering

abstract: The realization of integer and fractional Chern insulators in moiré systems provides a lattice setting for exploring how the structure of Bloch wave functions influences the interplay between topology and disorder. Here we investigate how layer-dependent disorder shapes Hall plateau widths and transitions. Using a realistic three-orbital model of twisted bilayer MoTe$_2$, we compare Hall and bulk transport under onsite-potential, displacement-field, and twist-angle disorder. At equal bare disorder strength, onsite-potential disorder produces broad integer plateaus with nearly direct transitions, whereas displacement-field disorder yields narrow plateaus separated by conducting regions with pronounced Hall-resistance dips. These contrasting behaviors arise from the layer composition of the Bloch states: contributions from different layer under displacement-field disorder partially cancel, weakening the bulk localization. Composite-fermion mean-field theory further yields fractional plateaus at $ν_h=2/3$ and $3/5$ with the same disorder dependence of plateau widths. These findings identify layer-dependent disorder as an important mechanism shaping Chern plateau stability in moiré systems beyond bare disorder strength alone.
comment: 5 pages, 4 figures in the main text and supplemental material
title: Integer and Fractional Chern Plateaus Shaped by Layer-Dependent Disorder

abstract: We investigate multiparameter quantum metrology and the energetic properties of an effective electron--proton spin system inspired by the hyperfine structure of the hydrogen atom. Considering the external magnetic field $\mathcal B$ and the hyperfine coupling strength $Λ$ as unknown parameters, we derive the quantum Fisher information matrix and establish the corresponding quantum Cramér--Rao bounds for their simultaneous estimation. We analyze the estimation precision and the correlations between the two parameters, showing that the weak-commutativity condition is satisfied despite the noncommutativity of the associated symmetric logarithmic derivatives. Independently, we explore the energetic properties of the system under a unitary charging protocol, characterizing its ergotropy, anti-ergotropy, storage capacity, and energy-basis coherence. We investigate the dependence of these quantities on the magnetic field, hyperfine coupling, temperature, and charging time. Our results provide a comprehensive characterization of the metrological properties and energetic performance of a hyperfine spin-based quantum system, highlighting its potential as a platform for quantum sensing and energy storage.
title: Quantum Metrology and Quantum Battery in a Hyperfine-Coupled Spin System

abstract: Spatially resolved magnetic-field imaging reveals material properties and local currents in microelectronic devices. Conventional pulsed scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry (SNVM) faces increasingly stringent microwave (MW) pulse-control requirements for detecting radio-frequency (RF) magnetic fields at frequencies ranging from tens to hundreds of megahertz. To address this challenge, we implement an RF-dressed continuous-wave (CW) sensing scheme for SNVM and demonstrate AC magnetic-field imaging at 33.5 MHz. The method exploits electron-spin double resonance in the NV spin-1 three-level system: the target RF magnetic field coherently couples two spin eigenstates, forming RF-dressed states whose splittings are detected in continuous-wave electron-spin double resonance (CW-ESDR) spectra under continuous laser, MW, and RF excitation. This approach avoids short, high-power MW pulses and synchronization between the RF field and a pulsed sensing sequence. Using an NV-ensemble diamond probe integrated with an atomic force microscope (AFM), we image the Oersted field of an RF-driven L-shaped microcircuit. Successively selecting three crystallographic NV axes by static bias-field control yields maps of RF magnetic-field projection magnitudes, with distinct distributions qualitatively reproduced by Biot-Savart calculations. Transverse bias-field control also tunes the RF-coupled spin-state transition frequency from 14.4 to 89.3 MHz, as characterized by spectroscopy and Hamiltonian analysis, with RF-dressed resonances directly observed in CW-ESDR spectra at 89.3 MHz. Together with previous RF magnetic-field detection up to 632 MHz using the same RF-dressed CW sensing principle in a confocal NV setup, these results support extending AC magnetic-field imaging with SNVM toward the hundreds-of-megahertz regime and, with additional phase information, vector magnetic-field reconstruction.
title: Axis-selective AC magnetic-field imaging in the tens-of-megahertz regime using RF-dressed continuous-wave scanning NV magnetometry

abstract: Quantum geometry plays a central role in shaping correlated phases in narrow bands, yet its influence on the competition between distinct magnetic orders, especially the emergence of altermagnetism, remains largely unexplored. To address this question, we study the quadrupole insulator model with strictly onsite generalized Hubbard-Kanamori interactions, in which both Néel antiferromagnetism and altermagnetism are symmetry-permitted. Depending on the parameters, the isolated narrow lowest band of the model can either be obstructed atomic with strong quantum geometry or trivial atomic with weak quantum geometry, while the dispersion is identical in the two cases. By partially filling the lowest band, our Hartree-Fock calculations show only conventional ferromagnetic phases for the weak quantum geometric case, while we find two collinear altermagnetic phases, as well as nematic phases, for the strong quantum geometric case. Such a dramatic difference can be understood by the distinct characters of the projected interaction: the projected interactions acquire sizable longer-range channels only for the strong quantum geometric case, while they are dominated by the on-site Hubbard channel in the weak quantum geometric case. These results establish the essential role of quantum geometry for altermagnetism to emerge from interacting narrow bands where crystalline symmetries cannot sufficiently constrain the magnetic order.
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures in the main text, 20 pages, 17 figures in the Supplemental Material
title: Narrow-Band Magnetism Allowed by Quantum Geometry: Altermagnetism and Beyond

abstract: Invertible topological phases of matter are described by gapped ground states of local Hamiltonians that are non-degenerate on any closed spatial manifold. Classification of invertible topological phases realized by bosonic or fermionic degrees of freedom is well-understood, particularly in low dimensions. In one-dimensional space, the classification can be understood through the boundary projective representations. We extend this paradigm to one-dimensional invertible topological phases of parafermionic degrees of freedom with symmetries. We define cohomological invariants that characterize distinct boundary projective representations and compute their stacking rules. Among other results, we show (i) how these cohomological invariants can be used to compute protected boundary degeneracy and (ii) how, in contrast to bosons or fermions, invertible phases of parafermions can form a non-Abelian group under stacking. For order-$N$ parafermions with $N$ a prime power, we define representative Hamiltonians realizing invertible topological phases with $\mathbb{Z}^{3}_{N}$ symmetry. We show that under stacking they generate a non-Abelian group of order $2N^3$. When $N$ is an odd prime, this group is $\mathrm{Heis}(\mathbb{Z}_N)\rtimes \mathbb{Z}^{\,}_{2}$, where $\mathrm{Heis}(\mathbb{Z}_N)$ is the Heisenberg group of order $N^{3}$.
title: Invertible parafermionic topological phases in one dimension

abstract: Multiterminal current measurements on a six-terminal Hall bar were recently used to argue that the current flow is chiral on the quantized Hall plateaus and non-chiral between them, and, in a companion analysis, that the imposed current flows along one edge only. We examine these conclusions with the self-consistent screening theory of the quantum Hall effect. The plateau values of the current partition follow from a vanishing longitudinal conductivity and a quantized Hall conductivity alone: every two-dimensional conductor with $σ_\ell=0$ and $σ_{\rm H}=νe^2/h$ has the conductance matrix of the "coherent and chiral" model, whatever the spatial distribution of the current. Terminal currents fix the current density only up to circulating currents, made explicit here with a stream function, and the chirality of the current density is a property of exactly this part. A two-dimensional local transport calculation for the measured device, including its two interior contacts, reproduces the plateau partition for all contact configurations and the ordering of the suppression between the plateaus without edge channels. The self-consistent current density separates into a chiral equilibrium (magnetization) current, which carries no net current, and a transport current that flows in the same direction in both edge strips; the "one-edge" imposed current is a bookkeeping choice of the reference chemical potential. The floating potentials of the two interior contacts are predicted to be equal when the bulk around them is quantized and to differ by up to half the Hall voltage when the current flows in edge strips. Multiterminal current partition measures the sign of the Hall conductivity and the absence of dissipation, not the location or the chirality of the transport current; the edge channels are the premise of the interpretation, not a result of the measurement.
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code, data and scripts reproducing every figure are in the ancillary file Supplemental_Material.zip. Submitted to Physical Review B
title: Chiral or unidirectional? Multiterminal current partition in the quantum Hall regime from self-consistent screening theory

abstract: Whether roton softening drives a continuous transition into a density-ordered or supersolid state is a longstanding question in interacting quantum fluids. Here, we address this microscopically in a mass-asymmetric electron--hole bilayer in which exciton condensation competes with interaction-driven crystallization. Using self-consistent Hartree--Fock--Bogoliubov theory and its time-dependent extension, we show that increasing the carrier-mass ratio or interlayer distance induces a pronounced roton minimum in the homogeneous exciton condensate liquid. The system undergoes a first-order transition to a crystalline state, preempting the roton instability. In this metastable regime, strongly interacting holes first drive the crystallization of the itinerant electrons, and the system then evolves into a hole-crystal--electron-metal phase at larger interlayer distance. Supersolid solutions with coexisting interlayer coherence and charge density order are also found to be energetically competitive near the crystallization boundary. We further discuss our findings based on recent experimental setups in two-dimensional material heterostructures.
title: Roton softening and crystallization in a mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayer

abstract: Quantum impurities and spin qubits are powerful local probes of magnetic fluctuations, but conventional relaxometry reduces their information to a local relaxation rate at a single frequency. Building on advances in two-qubit sensing of spatial correlations, we show how two complementary protocols probe finite-time correlations in interacting quantum matter. Phase-cycled Bell-state relaxometry isolates the signed contribution of correlated relaxation to the joint ground-state population. To second order in the probe-environment coupling, the resulting population contrast measures a finite-time integral of the energy-ordered cross-correlator. In the longitudinal regime, XY8 covariance probes the complementary symmetrized cross-correlator within a tunable frequency window. For a gapless quantum spin chain, the signals reveal interaction-dependent algebraic scaling and ballistic propagation. Luttinger-liquid theory links sign changes as the qubit frequency is swept to the propagation time between the probes. It also predicts distinct spatial power laws for the Bell signal before the correlation front and at late times, when the sensing window resolves the qubit frequency. Matrix-product-state calculations for the spin chain test the pre-front scaling at zero and finite magnetization and extract the propagation velocity from Bell oscillations at zero magnetization. The probe coupling geometry determines which spin and momentum sectors contribute to the measured signals.
title: Probing Spatiotemporal Quantum Correlations with Two-Qubit Relaxometry

abstract: State-of-the-art superconducting qubits rely on Al/AlO$_x$/Al Josephson junctions (JJs) as a nonlinear element with an ideal sinusoidal current-phase dependence, with its inductance set by the junction area and oxidation conditions. This idealization holds only if the many conduction channels through the amorphous AlO$_x$ barrier transmit weakly and almost identically. Here, we measure the second-order subgap Andreev current, which sets the second Josephson harmonic, in Al/AlO$_x$/Al JJs. For junction sizes relevant to qubits, we find that this current is dominated by $\lesssim 300$ effective channels whose transparencies exceed the ideal tunneling limit ($\lesssim 10^{-6}$) by orders of magnitude. For small and high-aspect-ratio junctions, increasing the junction size does not average out the effect of these high transparency channels but instead adds additional channels of even greater transparency. The trend inverts once both the width and length of the junction exceed a critical length scale, above which the effective transparency decreases with area. This non-ergodic scaling of the Andreev current is reproduced by simulations and attributed to non-self-averaging statistics of the transparency distribution, which arise from variations in oxide thickness. The effect is largely invisible to the normal-state conductance used to target the inductance and reveals unexpected geometric and size-related trade-offs for scaling superconducting qubit systems to large numbers of junctions.
comment: 35 pages including Supplementary Information; 5 figures and 1 table in the main text, 9 figures and 2 tables in the supplement
title: Non-ergodic Area Scaling of Andreev Transport in Al/AlO$_x$/Al Tunnel Junctions

abstract: When internal electrostatic stresses from electron repulsions overcome surface tension, charged nanoclusters elongate. However, the exact shape they reach at equilibrium has been unknown. We present an analytical model for the equilibrium structure of charged ellipsoidal nanoclusters via a free energy analysis. Energy maps are constructed that determine the equilibrium states as a function of cluster size, net charge, surface tension, and local curvature. The model is compared with molecular dynamics simulations of ice nanoclusters having solvated electrons. Despite the discreteness of the simulated atoms and electrons, both the predictions of the continuum analytical model for elongation and the equilibrium elongated shape show good agreement. The model could therefore predict nanocluster shape evolution in astrophysical and laboratory complex plasmas and atmospheric aerosols.
title: Equilibrium Elongation of Charged Nanoclusters

abstract: Low-temperature charged nanoclusters deform, primarily via surface diffusion, when surface electrostatic stresses and surface tension stresses are not balanced. We derive an analytical model for the kinetics of this process, based on the cluster size, net charge, surface tension, local curvature, temperature, and diffusivity. The model predicts the deformation time when either surface tension or electrostatic stress dominates, leading respectively to the collapse or elongation of the cluster. Comparison with molecular dynamics simulations of ice nanoclusters with solvated electrons shows quantitative agreement with a single fitted parameter. The model can predict the deformation kinetics of charged nanoclusters in atmospheric aerosols and complex plasmas.
title: Deformation Kinetics of Charged Nanoclusters via Surface Diffusion

abstract: Van der Waals magnets provide a versatile platform for exploring magnetic phenomena that emerge from reduced dimensionality, including layer-dependent magnetic ordering. Here, we use scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond magnetometry to measure the magnetization of a trilayer of the A-type antiferromagnet CrPS$_4$, resolving its zero-field bistability between the up-down-up ($\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow$) and down-up-down ($\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow$) layer magnetization configurations. The coercive field decreases approximately linearly with temperature, consistent with the Néel--Arrhenius model. Density Functional Theory calculations capture the temperature dependence of the magnetization and determine the coercive field in the coherent-rotation case. The measured coercive fields are lower, identifying thermally activated domain nucleation as the reversal mechanism. Spatial magnetic imaging supports this picture, revealing independently switching regions likely pinned by structural inhomogeneities. Our results highlight the power of scanning NV magnetometry for the quantitative investigation of magnetization reversal in two-dimensional magnets, unraveling the magnetic phenomenology that emerges in low-dimensional systems.
authors: Pieter C. J. A. van Zweeden
title: Thermally Activated Magnetic Switching in Antiferromagnetic Van der Waals Trilayers Resolved by Single-Spin Diamond Magnetometry

abstract: We investigate the topological phase diagram of a two-dimensional hole gas in planar germanium resulting from the combination of spin-orbit coupling, proximity-induced $s$-wave superconductivity, and magnetization. The peculiarity of the hole gas is the presence of a Rashba spin-orbit interaction cubic in momentum, possibly coexisting with a linear term, which results in the presence of distinct topological phases with Chern numbers as high as four. We map out the topological phase diagram based on effective single-band models with and without spin, and use input parameters based on a self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson calculation of a planar germanium hole gas. As a concrete model for inducing magnetization in the hole gas, we consider the exchange interaction coming from the presence of a dilute ensemble of manganese impurities. A topological phase with $C=3$ could be accessible experimentally in unstrained planar germanium.
title: Chiral topological phases of proximitized planar germanium

abstract: In this work we investigate the spectral evolution of topological domain-wall states in a one-dimensional structure described by the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model. We show that a local potential applied to the domain wall induces a selective coupling between a topological state and specific bulk states. Moreover, by increasing the gate potential, we observe that the domain wall state energies asymptotically reach a bulk band, whereas new domain wall states appear on the opposite side of the band. As a consequence, the domain-wall-state spectrum evolves through a sequence of localized states that remain separated from the bulk continuum. These effects are also reflected in transport calculations, where the conductance peaks follow the evolution of the energy spectrum. To experimentally verify these phenomena, we realize an RLC topo-electrical circuit and perform impedance spectroscopy measurements. We find that the impedance matches the local density of states, exhibiting resonances at frequencies associated with the bulk energies that selectively couple to the domain wall topological state.
title: Selective coupling and spectral evolution of topological domain-wall states under local perturbations

abstract: Read disturbance in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) depends on both local device interactions and the electrical conditions imposed by shared array circuitry. Here, we combine DIMM-level characterization results, device measurements, and TCAD simulations to interpret RowHammer, RowPress, and ColumnDisturb within a unified device-level physical framework. We relate charge evolution at the floating storage node to three key mechanisms: trap-assisted electron migration (EM), capacitive coupling (CC), and sense-amplifier-mediated disturb (SAMD). EM is local and trap-sensitive, while CC weakens with wordline separation. SAMD extends disturbance through shared column circuitry by modifying unselected-cell leakage under rail-level bitline biases, a contribution supported by the approximately ninefold higher OFF-state leakage measured relative to retention-like conditions for a high-voltage storage state. These distinct spatial ranges account for localized RowHammer and RowPress failures and remote ColumnDisturb populations with abrupt changes at subarray boundaries. We further interpret prolonged RowPress activation as a transition from an initial RowHammer-like transient to sustained leakage driven mainly by SAMD under held wordline and bitline biases. Within this device-level framework, trap effectiveness and storage-state-dependent leakage provide an interpretation of previously puzzling failure signatures, including the earlier onset of 0-to-1 RowHammer failures despite the predominance of 1-to-0 failures at high hammer counts. The same framework explains the observed RowPress and ColumnDisturb polarities and the duration-dependent reversal of neighboring- and passing-wordline effectiveness. These results provide a physical basis for developing compact DRAM reliability models across access patterns and array configurations.
title: A Unified Device-Level Physical Framework for DRAM Read Disturbance

abstract: A quantum correction to the rate of thermally activated transition between magnetic states is formulated within harmonic transition state theory and the Kramers-Langer theory by employing quantum statistics for stable spin-wave excitations around the initial state and the transition state. Quantum spin-wave statistics modifies both parameters of the Arrhenius expression for the transition rate relative to their classical values: the zero-point fluctuations renormalize the energy barrier, while the Bose-Einstein occupation of the spin-wave modes modifies the pre-exponential factor. Comparison of the classical and quantum-statistical pre-exponential factors reveals a systematic error associated with the excessive weight assigned to high-frequency excitations by classical equipartition. This error accumulates over the spin-wave spectrum and becomes increasingly severe with increasing dimensionality of the system. The effect is demonstrated for coherent magnetization reversal, and transitions involving noncollinear magnetic textures, including collapse of a magnetic skyrmion and rupture of a skyrmion tube, where classical and quantum-statistical predictions for the transition rate can differ by many orders of magnitude in three-dimensional systems.
title: Quantum spin-wave statistics and dimensionality in thermally activated magnetic transitions

abstract: The possibility of ambient-pressure superconductivity in $\mathrm{La_3Ni_2O_7}$ is theoretically explored via chemical substitution. Using first-principles and many-body calculations, we propose substituting $\mathrm{Ba}$ at the lanthanide site to exert chemical pressure, thereby mitigating the octahedral distortions that suppress superconductivity. Phonon calculations demonstrate the dynamical stability of the high-symmetry tetragonal phase in $\mathrm{La_{3-\it{x}}Ba_{\it{x}}Ni_2O_7}$ at a small doping ratio of $x \sim 0.15$. By applying the fluctuation exchange approximation to an effective model Hamiltonian derived from this stable structure, we calculate the Eliashberg eigenvalue $λ$ to evaluate the relative superconducting transition temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$ to existing unconventional superconductors. We conclude that $s_\pm$-wave superconductivity is likely to emerge, as the required $\mathrm{Ba}$ concentration ($x \sim 0.15$) is sufficiently small to minimize the detrimental suppression of superconductivity induced by hole doping.
title: Theoretical exploration of ambient-pressure superconductivity in the bilayer nickelate: A strategy of atomic substitution for tuning chemical pressure

abstract: We formulate a charge-$4e$ parafermionic-vortex route to qutrit processing as a conditional theory with explicit operational assumptions. Sector preservation and same-label charge-conjugation covariance imply closure for every adaptive visible record. For charge-conjugation-invariant inputs, record probabilities are independent of the supported reference state; for arbitrary inputs, discarding the reference gives a population-weighted mixture of conjugate sector maps. We give a finite-depth stability bound for complete labelled instruments, including postselection and initial zero-sector contamination. A self-contained calculation reproduces the known dense single-qutrit closure of the registered Clifford-plus-Flip gate set. We also specify an abstract ternary CSS $[[11,1,5]]_3$ syndrome/recovery decoder: 243 classical representatives per CSS component correct all 3,609 Pauli errors of support weight at most two, and an exact integer dynamic program yields the full independent-Pauli logical enumerator. Its all-syndrome acceptance is distinct from the known $1/1728$ ideal acceptance of one-round strange-state Golay distillation. An accepted-run target-infidelity budget and a synthetic parameter protocol expose the remaining noise assumptions. Native charge-$4e$ syndrome extraction, material feasibility, a device threshold, and unconditional fault tolerance are not established.
comment: Code and data included as ancillary files. Added related-work references and clarified model scope; results unchanged
title: Reference-Assisted Qutrit Control and Conditional One-Round Distillation in a Charge-4e Superconductor Model

abstract: Quantum fluctuations play a central role in superconductors by mediating the interactions that promote electron pairing and controlling the phase coherence required for macroscopic condensation. Thus far, understanding the interplay between quantum fluctuations and superconductivity remains challenging in unconventional superconductors. Here, we establish quantum phase fluctuations as the organizing principle linking superconductivity and Bose-insulating quantum criticality in a moiré flatband superconductor of alternating twisted trilayer graphene (ATTG). Superconductivity is optimal near half-filling of the moiré flatband and gives way to a density-wave-like resistance peak at high temperatures, in which we observe distinct temperature scales for the pairing (~6 K) and the condensation (~1 K). We observe compelling evidence of a bosonic superconducting quantum phase transition, driven by both out-of-plane and in-plane magnetic fields, with a universal critical resistivity of $R_c =~0.62R_Q$ and finite-temperature scaling of $zν_B = 2.3$, where $R_Q = h/4e^2$ is the quantum resistance for bosons. Strikingly, the observed bosonic insulator shows a nearly quantized resistivity of $R_Q$ that saturates at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, together with a zero-bias peak, a nearly zero Hall resistance, and a logarithmic dependence at higher temperatures. Both the superconductor and the bosonic insulator could be driven into the same critical quantum fluctuation regime dynamically under a large bias. Our results establish moiré flatband as a clean platform for studying unconventional superconductivity and bosonic quantum criticality governed by quantum fluctuations.
title: Quantum Fluctuations drive Emerging Bosonic Quantum Phases in a Moiré Flatband Superconductor

abstract: We investigate the influence of interfacial roughness amplitude and lateral periodicity on the chirality-dependent mobility of domain walls (DWs) in epitaxial Si(111)/Cu(2-7 nm)/Pd(3 nm)/Co(0.7 nm)/Pd(3 nm) heterostructures. By varying the Cu buffer layer thickness, we systematically modify the morphology of the magnetic interfaces while maintaining a constant composition and thickness of the Pd/Co/Pd trilayer. Scanning tunneling microscopy reveals that increasing the Cu thickness leads to the development of a hierarchical interfacial morphology characterized by increasing roughness amplitude and lateral periodicity. We observe a dramatic enhancement of the asymmetry between the velocities of DWs with opposite chirality in the creep regime, reaching a velocity ratio of approximately 50000 in the sample with a 7-nm-thick Cu buffer layer. This value exceeds by more than an order of magnitude the effective saturated asymmetry previously observed in Pd/Co/Pd structures with roughness controlled by the bottom Pd layer thickness. Despite comparable root-mean-square interface roughness in both series, the Cu-buffer-induced morphology exhibits a substantially larger characteristic lateral periodicity. We propose that the enhanced asymmetry originates from the different spatial organization of interfacial disorder, which modifies the pinning energy landscape and amplifies chirality-dependent thermally activated DW propagation. Our results suggest that engineering not only the amplitude but also the lateral spatial correlations of interfacial roughness provides an effective approach for controlling chiral DW dynamics in magnetic heterostructures.
title: Influence of interfacial roughness amplitude and periodicity on giant chiral asymmetry of domain wall mobility in epitaxial Cu/Pd/Co/Pd(111) films

abstract: Low-temperature heat-capacity data for pristine single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) bundles and for SWCNT/gas systems containing adsorbed Xe, Ne, N2, and CH4 were analyzed within a phenomenological framework. The data were fitted within the phenomenological form C(T) = C3T3 + C5T5, where the coefficients are interpreted as effective parameters of the coupled SWCNT-adsorbate excitation spectrum. Pristine SWCNT bundles exhibit a negative C5 coefficient, reflecting a non-Debye dispersive contribution associated with low-energy flexural-like modes. Gas adsorption systematically modifies both C3 and C5, indicating that the adsorbate's heat-capacity contribution may not be treated as fully independent. The Xe series suggests that mass loading, modified adsorbate-nanotube interaction, and changes in intertube coupling slightly reshape the nanotube vibrational response. Coverage-dependent measurements for Ne reveal a progressive shift from nanotube-dominated excitations toward domination of additional low-energy adsorbate modes in the phonon spectrum of the SWCNT-Ne system, while molecular adsorbates (N2, CH4) introduce translational, librational, orientational, and rotational degrees of freedom that generate correspondingly stronger perturbations.
title: Low-Temperature Heat Capacity of Single-Walled Carbon Nanotube Bundles with low dimensional gas systems

abstract: We investigate the use of strain-induced wrinkles in graphene nanoribbons to achieve tunable valley filtering and splitting, crucial for advancing valleytronic devices. By combining tight-binding simulations, strain tensor analysis, and quantum transport calculations, we explicitly demonstrate that wrinkle-induced pseudomagnetic fields facilitate current splitting and valley-selective filtering in folded graphene nanoribbons based on wrinkle parameters like height, strain spreading/deformation and wrinkle orientation (tilt angle). Moreover, we show that the application of a top-gate voltage provides dynamic control over valley splitting, allowing a continuous transition from well-separated valley currents to valley merging as the gate voltage increases. In other parameter regimes, valley filtering arises from an initial current-splitting mechanism, exhibiting a clear gate-controlled transition between distinct transport behaviors. Our results offer new insights into strain-engineered valley transport and suggest a promising pathway toward practical graphene-based valleytronic devices.
title: Tunable Valley Filtering and Splitting via Gate Control in Wrinkled Graphene

abstract: Topological nodal-line semimetals host drumhead surface states, carrying a large surface density of states. We show that these states support an acoustic surface plasmon, whose velocity is strongly enhanced by the Coulomb interaction. At sufficiently small wavevectors, the mode lies above the surface particle-hole continuum and below both mixed surface-bulk absorption thresholds, leaving bulk particle-hole creation as the leading damping channel. Near drumhead depletion, the dispersion is highly sensitive to the surface charge, which suggests applications of plasmon spectroscopy of nodal-line semimetals to sensing technologies.
title: Charge-tunable acoustic surface plasmons in topological nodal-line semimetals

abstract: Interfacial coupling in van der Waals two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offers an effective route to tailor the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of materials. Versatile control and precise engineering of such interlayer interactions can be further achieved through external parameters, like electric field, magnetic field, optical excitation, as well as layer stacking geometries. Here, we examined the magneto-optical properties of 2D semiconductor heterostructures made of antiferromagnetic CrSBr and a monolayer WS2, both of which host intriguing excitonic properties. We identified a type-II band alignment between these two layers and the magnetic proximity effects from CrSBr, manifested by an enhanced Zeeman valley splitting in the WS2 layer. The interlayer charge transfer shows strong spin selectivity and is governed by the relative alignment between the valley-spin polarization of photoexcited carriers in WS2 and the magnetization in CrSBr, giving rise to spin-sensitive circularly polarized photoluminescence (PL) from WS2. Furthermore, the highly anisotropic electronic dispersion in CrSBr enables stacking-dependent control of interlayer interactions, as inferred from a twist-angle dependence of PL quenching. Our work establishes a highly tunable 2D system that integrates valleytronics and magnetic excitons through multiple coupling channels, opening up new opportunities in all-optical manipulation of spin and magnon states and for the development of flexible spin-optoelectronic devices.
title: Tunable coupling between valley and magnetic excitons in WS2/CrSBr heterostructures

abstract: Magnetic topological insulator nanostructures are a promising platform for the realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation. For this, such nanostructures need to be embedded into the necessary superconducting architectures. In this study, we demonstrate a method for the growth of magnetic topological insulator nanostructures via molecular beam epitaxy, utilising digital alloying and defining their shapes in-situ by stencil mask technology. Cr-doped (Bi$_y$Sb$_{1-y}$)$_2$Te$_3$ micro- and nanometer-sized Hall bars are fabricated and the magneto-transport properties for various Cr doping amounts and different Hall bar dimensions are investigated at low temperatures. We find indications that the Fermi energy is located inside the bulk band gap, while disorder and charge puddles affect the transport behaviour. Furthermore, we investigate the magnetic properties and discuss the transition from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic behaviour.
title: Digitally-alloyed magnetic topological insulator nanostructures grown via stencil mask molecular beam epitaxy

abstract: Developing high-resistance quantized Hall resistance standards requires accessing values beyond the robust value seen in epitaxial graphene (R_{\mathrm{H}}=\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{h}{e^{2}}). This study evaluates the available parameter space of the coefficient of effective resistance across various epitaxial graphene p-n junction topologies, including rectangular, Corbino, and triangular layouts. Because mapping desired resistances to device configurations is mathematically degenerate, an automated Landauer-Büttiker Python solver was developed for all three topologies and was validated by cryogenic multi-terminal transport measurements and LTspice simulations. By analyzing the Shannon entropy of available states, it is found that rectangular checkerboards maximize topological complexity and tunable outputs, whereas Corbino geometries exhibit highly constrained resistance availabilities.
title: Quantized resistance limitations for graphene p-n junction devices

abstract: X-ray absorption spectroscopy and resonant inelastic X-ray scattering at the nitrogen K-edge show that the N$\equiv$N bond in N$_2$@C$_{60}$ is substantially more anharmonic than in free N$_2$, with the ground-state ($X^1Σ_g^+$) anharmonic constant $\hbarω_e x_e$ a factor of two larger ($3.8\pm0.3$~meV versus $\sim 1.8$~meV) despite an essentially unchanged harmonic frequency. The same enhancement is found across all three vibronic potentials accessible to the experiment---the electronic ground state, the core-excited intermediate state, and the spectator-decay final state---pointing to a common origin rather than an effect specific to one electronic configuration. High-level coupled-cluster calculations of the N$_2$@C$_{60}$ potential energy surface, however, find no significant change in anharmonicity upon encapsulation, ruling out a simple static distortion of the N$\equiv$N bonding potential by the fullerene cage. We propose instead that the dramatic increase in $\hbarω_e x_e$ above the gas-phase value -- which, taken literally, would imply an unphysical halving of the N$_2$ dissociation energy - reflects the breakdown of the single-molecule Morse description, as previously invoked to explain anomalous anharmonicities in N$_2$ clusters, and supported by the observation of shifts in the fullerene host's Raman modes.
title: Bond Anharmonicity in a Caged Molecule Probed by Vibronic Core Spectroscopy

abstract: Surface states are among the most striking consequences of band inversion in topological materials. In magnetotransport of three-dimensional topological insulators, the typical signature of surface state transport is a quantized Hall conductance with nontrivial sequences of integer filling factors, varying with the total carrier density. For two independent Dirac carriers, one expects Hall plateaus only at odd-integer filling factors. In this work, we report the observation of symmetry induced spin splitting in magnetotransport experiments on a dual-gate three-dimensional topological insulator device based on HgTe. In the topological surface state regime, we observe Hall plateaus at both odd and even integers when we gate the device symmetrically, i.e., with equal density at the top and bottom. This phenomenon originates in structural inversion symmetry, which remarkably induces a spin splitting and forces the eigenstates to be symmetric and antisymmetric linear combinations of the top and bottom surface states. This is in contrast with two-dimensional systems, where spin splitting is caused by absence of inversion symmetry. We interpret the experimental observations with a perturbative model using isoparity eigenstates, the conserved quantum number associated with structural inversion. The result demonstrates that the picture where the top and bottom states are treated as independent Dirac carriers is not valid when the carrier density is symmetric.
title: Symmetry induced spin splitting of topological surface states at equal carrier density

abstract: It is known that quasiparticles in the bulk of quantum Hall systems possess an emergent spin, which satisfies a spin-statistics relation. Recent results show that this spin can fractionalize: a quasiparticle spin in the bulk induces an opposite edge spin on the boundary. So far, the edge spin has only been studied in the simplest possible geometries, where the boundary is either circular or straight, without considering that a generic confining potential could give the droplet a non-symmetric shape. Yet, the value of the edge spin is not dictated by symmetry, but by topology: it is expected that the specific shape of the edge should not matter. In this work, we therefore generalize the edge spin to elliptically shaped droplets. We consider two different generalizations of the edge spin and test them on a family of elliptic Laughlin states introduced in the present work. The first, most straightforward, generalization is based on the properties of the single-particle orbitals for the elliptic confining potential. We show that this proposal applies to non-interacting states. The second proposal is based on the emergent properties of the quantum fluid. We show that this proposal also applies to interacting states, making it the suitable definition of the edge spin in the elliptic case. Our work demonstrates that it is possible to define an edge spin for Laughlin fluids with a non-trivial shape.
title: Edge spin generalization for quantum Hall Laughlin droplets with elliptic shapes

abstract: A magnetically gapped topological-insulator surface carries a half-quantized Hall response. We show that hybridizing the surface Dirac fermions with a flat band of chiral orbitals adds an integer to it: spin-momentum locking forces the hybridization to wind around the band-crossing ring, opening a topological gap. For orbitals with total angular momentum $j$, rotational symmetry fixes the surface Hall conductivity to $je^2/h$, with the sign set by the Dirac branch crossed and independent of the sign of the Dirac mass. The result survives crystal-field quenching of the orbital moment, with the winding then set by interference between hybridization pathways. First-principles calculations for a monolayer of nitric oxide adsorbed on Bi$_2$Se$_3$ predict a $\sim 20$ meV hybridization gap and an intrinsic surface Hall conductivity of $\frac{3}{2}e^2/h$, identifying molecular orbital angular momentum as a handle on surface topology.
title: Topological Hybridization Gaps from Molecular Orbitals Coupled to Dirac Fermions

abstract: Circularly dichroic resonant inelastic x-ray scattering has revealed electrically switchable $g$-wave phonon chirality in freestanding BaTiO$_3$ membranes. Here, we show from first principles that uniaxial strain changes the angular class of this texture. Lowering $C_{4v}$ to $C_{2v}$ adds a $d$-wave helicity that is bilinear in the orthorhombic strain $η$ and the polarization, with nodal lines along the stress axis. For the 38~meV branches at $η=1\%$, we find that (i) along the diagonal, where the helicity vanishes by symmetry without strain, it reaches about 60\% of the unstrained maximum, and (ii) at the measured wave vectors off the mirror it is reduced by more than half. With PBEsol and PBE+D3 force constants, the $d$-wave component grows linearly in $η$ and equals the $g$-wave one at $η^*\approx1.3\text{--}1.4\%$. Resolved by branch, the response of strain-split $E$ doublets is non-analytic in $η$, as captured by a two-band model. Strain therefore provides a second knob, besides the electric field, that controls the symmetry and the sign of phonon chirality in ferroelectric membranes.
title: Uniaxial strain induces $d$-wave phonon chirality in ferroelectric BaTiO$_3$

abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.
title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures

abstract: Recently, an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with three atoms per unit cell has been experimentally realized in perovskite exciton-polariton micropillars. A distinctive feature of this system is that the second and third bands undergo a topological transition through a band crossing at the wave vector $k=0$, associated with a negative coupling. In this work, we analytically determine the phase diagram of the model as a function of the on-site energy splitting and the ratio of intercell to intracell hopping amplitudes. We identify seven regions in this lane, with four distinct topological phases, characterized by different Zak phases of the three bands. Our results provide a useful theoretical framework for interpreting existing experiments and serve as a guide for future experimental investigations of this system.
title: Topological phase diagram of an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with negative coupling

abstract: We study entanglement generation between two spin qubits mediated by a single, thermally mixed, high-spin ($S=5/2$) magnetic impurity, using the Lindblad master equation to compare coherent and dissipative control of the mediator. We show that no coherent drive, however strong or resonant, can purify the mediator beyond its thermal value --- a direct consequence of unitary evolution exactly preserving state purity --- while a dissipative channel purifies it up to the limit set by the optical pumping cycle itself, $\mathrm{Tr}[ρ_M^2]\approx0.8$. Modeling this channel with rates fixed by the measured optical pumping of a single Mn spin, we find that the entanglement it enables is not monotonic in the pump strength: it peaks at a finite rate and then decreases, since the same channel leaks decoherence to the qubits through the coupling that mediates their entanglement. At the experimental pumping rate, a single $80$ns pulse purifies the mediator, the resulting polarization persists for a timescale three orders of magnitude longer than the entangling dynamics, and the first-recurrence negativity rises from $0.18$ to $0.64$ at $12$K, remaining above $0.6$ up to $30$K. These results establish dissipation, not as noise to be suppressed, but as the very resource that makes robust entanglement generation possible.
title: Dissipation as a Resource for Entanglement via High-Spin Mediator Purification

abstract: Fibonacci anyons support universal topological quantum computation. They have been proposed to emerge in fractional quantum Hall (FQH) systems, such as the filling-fraction $ν=\tfrac{2}{3}$ state described by an effective $SU(3)_2$ Chern-Simons theory, and the $ν=\tfrac{2}{5}$ state with a $3$-cluster structure (an $n$-cluster structure means that $n$-electron bound states form a Laughlin-type wave function of the form $(z^{(n)}_i-z^{(n)}_j)^m$). In this work, we systematically classify FQH wave functions $P(z_1,\ldots,z_N)$ in the $N\rightarrow\infty$ limit, through a generalized pattern of zeros (gPOZ) approach, where the wave function is determined by the leading order of zero along with the accompanying leading polynomial that develops as successive number of $z_i$'s are brought together. Within this approach, we obtain a $(ν,h,c)$-classification of wave functions with a $2$-cluster (pair) structure. Among these wave functions, those with $(h,c) = (\tfrac12,\tfrac12)$, $(\tfrac32,\tfrac{7}{10})$, $(3,\tfrac45)$ correspond to gapped FQH states with filling fraction $ν$ and edge-state chiral central charge $c+1$, while others with $c<0$ may be gapless. We find that even a $2$-cluster structure can give rise to Fibonacci statistics, for $(ν,h,c) = (\tfrac14,\tfrac32,\tfrac{7}{10})$, corresponding to the $(5,4)$ minimal model, and for $(ν,h,c) = (\tfrac17,3,\tfrac45)$, corresponding to the $(6,5)$ minimal model. We further construct an ideal $4$-body Hamiltonian whose ground state is the $(\tfrac14,\tfrac32,\tfrac{7}{10})$ state.
title: Fibonacci Non-Abelian Quantum Hall States with Pair Structure - a classification of chiral 2-cluster many-body wave-functions

abstract: Wigner solids and crystals are many-body phases of matter in which repulsive interactions between the charge carriers cause them to freeze into a solid. How Wigner solids compete or cooperate with integer and fractional quantum Hall liquids has been a long-standing open question. Here, we investigate this question for zero-field, electron and hole Wigner solids in cadmium arsenide quantum wells. In the low temperature limit, our results are consistent with a recent theoretical model [A. P. Reddy and L. Fu, Phys. Rev. B 113, L161403 (2026)] that proposes that the quantum Hall liquid can become energetically favored over the solid at low integer filling factors. Going beyond the low-temperature limit, we observe a re-entrant solid that emerges from the quantum Hall liquid. We explain this observation by considering the role of spin entropy, in close analogy with the zero-field Pomeranchuk effect, but appearing here at finite fields. The competition between quantum Hall liquids and Wigner solids is thus governed by both energy and entropy terms, giving rise to rich phase stability diagrams that result from the interplay between topology and correlations.
comment: Accepted for publication in npj Quantum Materials
title: Quantum melting and Pomeranchuk effect of zero-field Wigner solids

abstract: A spin wave in a filling-one quantum Hall ferromagnet is neutral but carries an electric dipole perpendicular to its momentum. A spatially periodic electrostatic potential therefore creates parallel channels for spin waves. We use this established mechanism to calculate how confinement changes the exchange binding of magnons travelling in the same direction. Narrower channels increase the overlap of their transverse wavefunctions and strengthen the effective attraction. In an isolated harmonic channel, the energy required to remove one magnon from a cluster of $N$ is $π(k_*\ell)^4N(N-1)/4$ times the transverse level spacing to leading order, where $k_*$ is the mean wave number along the channel and $\ell$ is the magnetic length. We predict the frequency and momentum dependence of the spectral line for adding a second magnon to one already present, both in an isolated channel and in a coupled array. Tunnelling in a wide array can make the binding energy exponentially small, while a strip narrower than the transverse pair size recovers one-dimensional binding at sufficiently weak attraction. We also find that a moving potential can carry a single wave packet with less spreading than free propagation when its initial group velocity matches the potential's speed.
title: Magnon binding in a quantum Hall ferromagnet with a periodic electric field

abstract: Ge-based super-semi heterostructures are a promising platform for implementing Andreev spin qubits (ASQs). For example, they can be isotopically purified to eliminate nuclear spins that cause decoherence. However, spin-orbit coupling (SOC), which is a key ingredient for ASQs, is cubic in momentum for hole-based materials like Ge, in contrast with more-conventional ASQ materials (e.g., InAs wires), for which the SOC is linear in momentum. In this work, we study the interplay between geometrical properties like the channel width, and gate-tunable properties like the chemical potential, on ASQ operations. Intriguingly, we find that the spin splitting in a planar Ge Josephson junction does not depend on the junction width, in contrast with InAs nanowires. We explore the possibility of exploiting this property to suppress the harmful effects of charge traps. However, this prospect is spoiled by the fact that charge traps also affect the chemical potential, in addition to the channel width. Our results provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms governing spin splitting in ASQs and offer guidance for optimizing ASQs in other materials with cubic SOC.
title: Gate-tunable spin splitting for Andreev spin qubits in Ge quantum well heterostructures

abstract: From a canonical quantisation approach of macroscopic quantum electrodynamics, we derive the interaction Hamiltonian due to a dipole emitter interacting with a time-symmetry-broken topological insulator (TSB-TI), described by an axionic coupling Lagrangian. This provides an additional interaction term dependent on the magneto-electric coupling strength inherent to the TSB-TI which will modify measurements on related observables. The spontaneous decay rate is calculated in the Born-Markov approximation for a general electromagnetic Green's tensor, and then specifically for the case of a planar parallel-plate cavity.
title: Hidden Momenta due to Magneto-Electric Coupling in Non-Reciprocal Media

abstract: Antiferromagnetic (AFM) spin Hall oscillators offer an electrical route to compact terahertz sources, while AFM spin Hall diodes can be used as a promising detectors of terahertz signals, however, their attainable frequency and the redout efficiency are constrained by the dynamics of a single AFM layer. We theoretically and numerically investigate a spin Hall multilayer junction Pt/AFM/Pt/AFM/Pt comprising two canted AFM layers, driven by independent drive DC currents flowing in the outer platinum (Pt) layers. Using a model based on the coupled Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert-Slonczewski equations for four AFM sublattices and a phase-dependent two-interface spin Hall magnetoresistance model, we show that the device manifests itself as a DC current-driven oscillating spin Hall magnetoresistance. When an additional DC (AC) signal current is applied to the junction, the device generates an output AC (DC) voltage. Our model predicts current-driven, locked, co- and counter-rotational states of the net magnetization at Neel-vector frequencies in the top and bottom AFM layers, respectively. These states result in a multi-frequency response of the spin Hall magnetoresistance at the sum and difference frequencies. The counter-rotation regime additionally activates the phase-sensitive mixing contribution, producing a fourth harmonic. In contrast, the co-rotation regime provides a difference-frequency channel on the order of 100 GHz, although mutual locking prevents this output from being tuned continuously toward zero. Our estimations show that the device matched to an external load can generate output AC power of 1.2 nW at the second harmonic and 0.8 pW at the fourth harmonic, and can produce a DC voltage of about 1 mV for a 6 mA input signal current.
title: Tunable Multi-Frequency-Band Generator and Detector of AC Signals Based on a Spin Hall Device with Two Antiferromagnetic Layers

abstract: Unconventional magnets host momentum-dependent spin splitting without spin-orbit coupling. We demonstrate that the combination of nonlinear spin polarisation and spin photocurrent is a powerful diagnostic tool for probing the spin space group symmetry, magnetic domain, and quantum geometry in unconventional magnets, providing information beyond their equilibrium spin texture. We develop a mechanism-resolved joint symmetry analysis of second-order spin photoresponse tensors and analyse their frequency dependence, magnetic parity and relaxation scaling. We show that unconventional magnets are natural platforms to achieve large magnetic-even spin photocurrent induced by unpolarised light, making them promising candidates for polariser-free spin sources. We present numerical illustrations for prototypical hybrid parity and odd parity magnet models. Our work provides optical fingerprints connecting spin-space symmetry to distinct microscopic pathways of spin accumulation and transport.
title: Nonlinear spin generation and spin photocurrent as a symmetry and magnetic domain probe in unconventional magnets

abstract: We theoretically propose chiral-phonon-mediated spin current injection into an Ising superconductor in a chiral-insulator/Ising-superconductor heterostructure, where nonequilibrium phonons driven by a temperature gradient transfer their angular momentum to electron spins via interfacial phonon-spin conversion. Using the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism, we derive an expression for the injected spin current and show that it depends on the difference between the contributions from the two phonon branches with opposite circular polarizations. We further investigate the temperature dependence of the injected spin current density at different in-plane magnetic field strengths. In the superconducting state, the spin current density increases with temperature or in-plane magnetic field strength. In addition to the kink at the superconducting transition, a second kink appears below the transition temperature. The position of this kink is consistent with the onset of phonon-induced two-quasiparticle excitations as the superconducting gap decreases with increasing temperature. We further investigate the magnetic-field dependence of the kink temperature in a temperature--magnetic-field phase diagram.
title: Chiral-phonon-mediated spin current injection into an Ising superconductor

abstract: Strongly interacting quantum systems display puzzling electrical transport properties whose interpretation remains controversial. Many theoretical and phenomenological analyses assume that the complex behaviour observed in such `quantum materials' originates either from quasi-particles dressed with an anomalous electron self-energy or from collective excitations associated with hydrodynamic flow. Despite their distinctly different starting points, the underlying assumption is that dissipation of electrical current arises from the relaxation of the total momentum of charge carriers. This classical description breaks down in the absence of long-lived charge carriers. In such strange metals dissipation seems to be governed by the rate at which equilibrium is thermally restored, and it has been suggested that this constitutes an upper bound, known as the `Planckian limit'. Here we show that in this quantum regime a description of the conductivity in terms of relaxation rates no longer suffices: strange metal transport is carried instead by fast-decaying current fluctuations, which together with quantum detailed balance give rise to the widely observed Planckian dissipation. The distinction between classical and quantum metals becomes transparent when experimental data is analysed in terms of the current-current correlation function instead of the optical conductivity. When applied to the cuprate superconductors, such analysis uncovers that the strange metal response is present at all doping levels, and that a second, classical component develops above optimal doping. This simple, but powerful, approach further highlights essential features associated with superconductivity, (pseudo-)gaps, provides fresh insight in the properties of metals, and identifies key areas where progress in our theoretical understanding is needed.
title: Optical response of quantum metals

abstract: In non-Hermitian (NH) fermionic chains with spatially random imaginary gauge fields, single-particle eigenstates exhibit erratic NH skin localization with strongly fluctuating, subexponential decay, distinct from both conventional skin accumulation and Anderson localization. At finite filling, Pauli exclusion suppresses macroscopic accumulation and instead leads to fragmentation of the particle density, in sharp contrast to Hermitian disordered systems. Using exact free-fermion methods, we show that the density organizes into disconnected regions of high and low occupancy, forming spatially separated Fermi domains whose number $N_{\mathrm{FS}}$ scales subextensively with system size $L$. Remarkably, fragmentation is not only an equilibrium property but also emerges dynamically in the NH evolution, unlike in Hermitian systems where such structures are not dynamically selected. This behavior admits a Coulomb-gas description in a stochastic potential, establishing a direct link between erratic NH skin localization and real-space fragmentation of many-body states.
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, accepted for publication in Phys. Rev.B, Supplemental document not included
title: Fragmentation in Non-Hermitian Many-Body Systems

abstract: We study the nonequilibrium state generated by a real Ohmic contact (ROC) in the charge-fractionalization regime. We then investigate its thermal-energy relaxation along a quantum Hall edge mediated by a fictitious Ohmic contact (FOC) with large capacitance and perfect coupling to the edge. For cold Ohmic contacts, the electron distribution function and current noise are fully described by their equilibrium forms and the corresponding Fermi-Dirac distribution. In contrast, in the case of hot Ohmic contacts, strong thermalization effects do not drive the outgoing state into complete equilibrium. Both the distribution function and the noise retain signatures of the initial nonequilibrium state and therefore cannot be characterized solely by the effective contact temperature, contrary to common assumptions.
title: Thermal-energy relaxation in chiral quantum Hall edge mode

abstract: For dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in open chains it has been noted that the boundary can change the bulk: in time windows bounded by DQPTs, exponentially localized edge modes of the Loschmidt matrix produce a finite change in the intensive return rate. These modes have been attributed to topological properties of the initial and final Hamiltonians. Here we show that it is not the topology of the Hamiltonians but rather that of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix which protects these edge modes. In particular, we show that topological edge modes can exist in class A, where both Hamiltonians are topologically trivial. For classes A, BDI, and AIII we show that these modes are protected by $\mathbb{Z}$ indices of a Toeplitz operator and that K-splitting theorems provide a precise bulk-boundary correspondence. In class D, they are protected instead by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index that records whether the quench has flipped the fermion parity at the edge. The bulk invariant for class D can be formulated either as a ratio of the Loschmidt amplitudes for periodic and anti-periodic boundary conditions or as a winding number that counts phase vortices in momentum and time. We discuss examples and provide numerical data for all four topological classes.
title: When the Boundary Changes the Bulk: Topological Edge Modes in Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions

abstract: Matching the Coulomb and logarithmic limits of the Rytova--Keldysh model gives a universal zero-field spectrum for monolayer exciton $s$ states, $E_n\simeq-\mathrm{Ry}^*/[n-1/2+f_n(ξ)]^2$, where $ξ$ is the screening parameter. Analytical radii determine diamagnetic coefficients and the magnetic crossover scale. Zero-field deviations peak near $1\%$ across the full screening range $0\leqξ\leq100$. For the sampled hBN-encapsulated monolayers, magnetoexciton energies agree with numerical spectra to sub-meV rms up to $100\T$ and capture the measured orbital shifts. Shared parameters link optical and magneto-optical spectra.
title: Universal Analytical Description of Magnetoexcitons in Two-Dimensional Semiconducting Materials

abstract: Finite-wave-vector electromagnetic fields provide a route to accessing nonlocal collective dynamics in two-dimensional electron systems. Here, we theoretically investigate the magnetoplasmon response of a two-dimensional electron system subjected to a spatially nonuniform electromagnetic field in a perpendicular magnetic field. By combining Maxwell's equations with the Kubo formula, we derive the nonlocal magnetoconductivity tensor and obtain the self-consistent dispersion relation for collective modes. We show that a finite in-plane wave vector enables higher-order cyclotron transitions, allowing higher harmonics of the cyclotron resonance to contribute to the nonlocal conductivity. These harmonics hybridize with the magnetoplasmon mode, producing avoided crossings in the collective-mode spectrum characteristic of Bernstein modes.
